title: the friend test
subtitle: the voice already used for others

steps.text: most of us are much kinder to friends than to ourselves.
picture a good friend telling you this:

steps.quote: i'm so stupid. i failed the exam.
steps.label: your friend

steps.text: what would you say to them?

options.label: one exam isn't you
options.reply: kind and true. you already know how to do this.

options.label: that sounds rough, want to talk?
options.reply: warm, and it leaves room for them. you already know how to do this.

options.label: you studied really hard
options.reply: that's seeing the effort, not just the result. the skill is already there.

steps.text: now imagine it happened to you. what would the inner voice say?

options.label: probably something harsh
options.reply: most people say that. the gap between those two voices is what we're working with.

options.label: about the same as for a friend
options.reply: that's lovely. you have a friend in there already.

options.label: not sure
options.reply: that's okay. next time it happens, just listen for it.

steps.text: people sometimes worry that being kind to themselves will make them lazy. research suggests the opposite.
in one set of studies, people who took a kind view of a mistake were more motivated to improve, and studied longer for a retest.

steps.prompt: think of something that's been weighing on you. what would a good friend hear from you?
ideas: one bad day isn't who they are.
they're being harder on themselves than they deserve.
it makes sense they feel that way, and it isn't the whole story.
they're allowed to mess up and still be loved.

steps.text: talking inward like a friend isn't soft. it helps people keep going.
once today, notice the gap: the words for a friend, and the words used inward.

grounding.idea: self-compassion after a setback increased motivation to improve
grounding.source: Breines & Chen, 2012, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

grounding.idea: writing to yourself as a compassionate friend
